text: Google Chrome is a cross-platform web browser developed by Google, launched in 2008 for Microsoft Windows, built using free software components from Apple WebKit and Mozilla Firefox. Versions were later released for Linux, macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and Android, where it is currently the default browser. The browser is also the main component of ChromeOS, serving as the platform for web applications. Most of Chrome's source code comes from Google's open-source project Chromium, but Chrome is licensed as proprietary freeware. Initially using the WebKit rendering engine, Google forked it in 2013 to create the Blink engine, which all Chrome variants except iOS used as of 2017. As of December 2025, StatCounter estimates Chrome has a 75.23% worldwide browser market share on personal computers, is the most-used browser on tablets and smartphones, and holds a 71.22% market share across all platforms combined, making it the most-used web browser globally. Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page spearheaded a software demonstration using Mozilla Firefox developers, which convinced CEO Eric Schmidt—initially opposed to entering the browser market due to concerns about "bruising browser wars" and Google's size—to prioritize Chrome as a core business, leading to its commercial success. Schmidt stated that the demonstration was so good it "essentially forced me to change my mind." Rumors of Google developing a browser first appeared in September 2004, following the rise of Mozilla Firefox 1.0 and Internet Explorer's security issues. Chrome development began in 2006 and was spearheaded by Sundar Pichai. The browser was first publicly released as a beta version on September 2, 2008, for Windows XP and newer with support for 43 languages, and later released as a stable version on December 11, 2008. A passage in the initial beta's Terms of Service granting Google a license to all content transferred via Chrome was criticized and removed after being inherited from general Google terms. Chrome quickly gained about 1% usage share, dropped to 0.69% in October 2008, then rose back above 1% by December 2008. Google planned to release versions for macOS and Linux in early 2009, with developer previews announced on June 4, 2009, and beta versions released in December 2009. Chrome 5.0, announced on May 25, 2010, was the first stable release supporting all three platforms. Chrome was one of twelve browsers offered on BrowserChoice.eu for European Economic Area Windows users in 2010. Chrome was assembled from 25 code libraries, including Mozilla's Netscape Portable Runtime, Network Security Services (dropped in version 45), Skia Graphics Engine, SQLite, and others, with the V8 JavaScript engine, developed by a team in Denmark led by Lars Bak, being a key component due to its performance benefits for web applications like Gmail. Chrome initially used WebKit, then forked it to create Blink in 2013, using only WebKit's WebCore components while replacing other parts like its multi-process architecture. Chrome is internally tested with unit testing, automated user action testing, fuzz testing, and WebKit layout tests (99% passed), as well as against commonly accessed websites within 20–30 minutes. Google created Gears for Chrome to add web application features like offline support, which were later replaced by HTML5 standards. In March 2011, Google introduced a simplified logo to reflect Chrome's focus on a clutter-free, easy-to-use web experience. On January 11, 2011, Chrome removed H.264 video codec support for its HTML5 player to align with open codecs in the Chromium project, though hardware-accelerated H.264 decoding was added in November 2012. In October 2013, Cisco open-sourced its H.264 codecs. On February 7, 2012, Google launched Chrome Beta for Android 4.0 devices, and on many new Android 4.1+ devices, Chrome became the default browser. In May 2017, Google announced a version of Chrome for augmented and virtual reality devices. Chrome features a minimalistic interface, including the merging of the address and search bars into the omnibox. The first release passed Acid1 and Acid2 tests, and from version 4.0 passed all aspects of Acid3, though as of April 2017 it no longer passes Acid3 due to evolving web standards. In May 2011, Chrome scored 10 failed/11,578 passed in the ECMAScript Test 262 (ES5.1), outperforming Firefox 19 (193 failed) and Internet Explorer 9 (600+ failed), with IE10 scoring 7 failed. On the W3C CSS 2.1 test suite, Chrome's rendering engine passed 89.75% of tests. On the HTML5 test, Chrome 41 scored 518 out of 555, ahead of the five most popular desktop browsers, with Chrome 41 on Android scoring 510 out of 555, and Chrome 44 scoring 526, just 29 points below the maximum. The default interface includes back, forward, refresh/cancel, and menu buttons, with a home button available via Settings. Tabs are positioned at the top of the window, and can be transferred between containers by dragging. Each tab includes an omnibox with URL and search functions. When a user types in the omnibox, Chrome provides suggestions based on visited sites, popular websites, and searches, with instant suggestions based on visited sites not being turnable off. If keywords are typed and Enter is pressed, a search is conducted using the default search engine. The New Tab Page displays thumbnails of the most visited sites, frequent searches, bookmarks, and recently closed tabs, with features like rearranging, pinning, and removing thumbnails, and a "Recently closed" bar and "tips" section. Starting with version 3.0, users can install themes to customize the browser, with many free themes available in an online gallery. Chrome includes a bookmarks submenu with access to the Bookmark Manager and a toggle for the bookmarks bar. On January 2, 2019, Google introduced Native Dark Theme for Chrome on Windows 10. In 2023, Chrome was completely revamped using Google's Material You design language, including more rounded corners, dynamic color systems similar to Android 12, a revamped address bar, new icons and tabs, and a simplified 3-dot menu. Starting with version 4.1, Chrome included a built-in translation bar using Google Translate, available for 52 languages, which prompts users to translate when a foreign language is detected. Chrome allows users to synchronize bookmarks, history, and settings across devices via a chosen Google Account, updating all signed-in instances. For web developers, Chrome includes an element inspector to examine a webpage's DOM structure. Chrome has special URLs that load application-specific pages and a built-in feature to enable experimental functions, originally called about:labs and later renamed to about:flags. The desktop edition can save pages as HTML with assets in a "_files" subfolder or as unprocessed HTML-only documents, or in MHTML format. Users can create local desktop shortcuts to open web applications without the regular interface, allowing web apps to run alongside local software. This feature was enhanced with the Chrome Web Store, launched on December 7, 2010, allowing users to install web applications as extensions. In September 2013, Google introduced Chrome apps "For your desktop," enabling offline access, desktop shortcuts, and less dependence on Chrome, with apps launching in separate windows resembling native applications. The Chrome Web Store, opened on February 11, 2011, with Chrome 9.0, allows users to install extensions and apps, with themes and extensions integrated into a searchable catalog. Browser extensions can modify Chrome, are supported on desktop but not mobile, and are written using HTML, JavaScript, and CSS, distributed through the Chrome Web Store. Extensions include accessibility features like Google Tone, which uses speakers to share URLs with nearby devices. Extensions were enabled by default on the developer channel in September 2009, with a beta gallery launching in December with about 300 extensions, expanding to approximately 1,500 by January 2010. In 2014, Google began restricting Windows users from installing extensions not hosted on the Chrome Web Store, expanding this to all Windows and Mac users in 2015 after reporting a 75% drop in customer support requests for uninstalling unwanted extensions. In October 2018, Google introduced Manifest V3, a major update to the extension API that modernizes the architecture, improves security and performance, uses declarative APIs to reduce broad access, replaces background pages with limited "Service Workers," and prohibits remotely-hosted code. This change drew criticism for limiting ad blockers' ability to check rules and update filter lists independently. The V8 JavaScript engine used by Chrome features dynamic code generation, hidden class transitions, and precise garbage collection. In 2008, several websites conducted benchmark tests using the SunSpider JavaScript Benchmark and Google's own computationally intense benchmarks, including ray tracing and constraint solving, which unanimously reported Chrome's performance.

Google announced a major update to Chrome's extension API known as "Manifest V3," which modernizes the extension architecture to improve security and performance by adopting declarative APIs to reduce broad access and enable more efficient browser implementations, replacing background pages with feature-limited "Service Workers" to lower resource usage, and prohibiting remotely-hosted code. This change drew criticism because it restricts the number of rules and types of expressions that ad blockers can check and prevents independent updates to ad-blocking filter lists. Chrome uses the V8 JavaScript engine, which includes features such as dynamic code generation, hidden class transitions, and precise garbage collection. In 2008, benchmark tests using SunSpider and Google's own computationally intensive benchmarks—such as ray tracing and constraint solving—showed Chrome outperformed competitors including Safari (Windows), Firefox 3.0, Internet Explorer 7, Opera, and Internet Explorer 8; however, by October 11, 2010, independent tests revealed Chrome was scoring behind Opera's Presto engine after version 10.5. Mozilla claimed its TraceMonkey JavaScript engine (in beta) was faster than Chrome's V8 in some tests, with John Resig noting Chrome's strong performance on recursion-intensive benchmarks but questioning whether Google's suite reflected real-world applications, citing Firefox 3.0's poor performance due to missing recursion-tracing. Two weeks after Chrome's 2008 launch, the WebKit team introduced SquirrelFish Extreme, which reported a 36% speed improvement over V8. Chrome uses DNS prefetching to speed up website lookups, a feature shared with Firefox, Safari, Internet Explorer (via DNS Pre-resolution), and Opera (as a UserScript). Chrome previously used the SPDY protocol instead of HTTP for servers supporting it, such as Google services, Facebook, and Twitter, but SPDY support was removed in Chrome version 51 due to its replacement by HTTP/2. In November 2019, Google began developing "speed badging" systems to inform users why pages load slowly, with no release date provided. Chrome once had a Data Saver feature called Lite Mode, which automatically lazy-loaded images and iframes to speed up page loads, announced by engineers Addy Osmani and Scott Little; however, Lite Mode was disabled in Chrome 100 due to a decrease in mobile data costs in many countries. Chrome periodically retrieves updates from two blacklists—one for phishing and one for malware—and warns users when visiting flagged sites; this service is also available via the free public "Google Safe Browsing API." Chrome uses a process-allocation model to sandbox tabs, applying the principle of least privilege so that each tab process cannot access critical memory functions or interact with other tab processes, similar to Microsoft's "Protected Mode" in Internet Explorer 9 and later; on Linux, this uses seccomp mode. In January 2015, TorrentFreak reported that using Chrome with a VPN could pose serious security risks due to WebRTC support. On September 9, 2016, Chrome 56 introduced warnings for visiting insecure HTTP websites to encourage migration to HTTPS. On December 4, 2018, Google released Chrome 71 with new security features, including a built-in ad-blocking system and a plan to combat websites that enable involuntary mobile subscription sign-ups. On September 2, 2020, Chrome 85 extended support for Secure DNS on Android, enabling automatic switching to DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) when the DNS provider supports it. Since 2008, Chrome has been criticized for lacking a master password to protect user passwords; developers argue it does not provide meaningful security against determined attackers and have refused to implement one, with related bugs marked "WontFix"; as of February 2014, Chrome requires the user to enter their Windows account password before showing saved passwords. On Linux, Chrome/Chromium stores passwords in three ways: GNOME Keyring, KWallet, or plain text, with automatic selection based on the desktop environment; passwords in GNOME Keyring or KWallet are encrypted and protected by dedicated daemons, while plain text passwords are not; previously stored unencrypted passwords are automatically moved to encrypted stores when these services are used; support for GNOME Keyring and KWallet was added in version 6 and became the default in version 12. As of version 45, Chrome's password manager is no longer integrated with Keychain due to lost interoperability. No Chrome security vulnerabilities were exploited in the 2009–2011 Pwn2Own events; at Pwn2Own 2012, a French team exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in the Flash version bundled with Chrome to gain full control of a fully patched 64-bit Windows 7 machine via a booby-trapped website that bypassed Chrome's sandboxing. Chrome was also compromised twice at the 2012 CanSecWest Pwnium; Google's response, delivered by Jason Kersey, praised the researchers and noted the exploits were "works of art," with fixes deployed within 10 hours of submission. A significant number of Chrome vulnerabilities stemmed from Adobe Flash Player; for example, the 2016 Pwn2Own attack on Chrome relied on four vulnerabilities—two in Flash, one in Chrome, and one in the Windows kernel. In 2016, Google announced plans to phase out Flash Player in Chrome, beginning with version 53, initially disabling it for ads and background analytics, with the ultimate goal of full disablement by the end of the year, except on sites deemed broken without it; Flash was later re-enabled on a site-by-site basis excluding ads and analytics. Leaked documents from 2013 to 2016, codenamed Vault 7, detail the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency's capabilities, including the ability to compromise web browsers like Chrome. Google introduced download scanning protection in Chrome 17; in February 2018, it added an ad-blocking feature based on Interactive Advertising Bureau recommendations, giving sites employing invasive ads a 30-day warning before blocking their ads; Consumer Reports advised users to install dedicated ad-blocking tools for better protection against malware and tracking. Incognito mode prevents Chrome from storing local history, cookies, site data, or form inputs, though downloaded files and bookmarks are saved; user activity remains visible to websites and Internet service providers. Incognito mode is similar to private browsing in other browsers and does not prevent saving across all windows—users can switch between incognito and regular windows, with only the incognito window operating in private mode. The iOS version of Chrome supports locking incognito tabs with Face ID, Touch ID, or device passcode; in 2022, Google began implementing this feature on Android versions, now available on Android 12 and above if hardware supports it. In 2024, Google agreed to destroy billions of records to settle a lawsuit alleging it secretly tracked internet use of users who believed they were browsing privately in incognito mode. In February 2012, Google introduced the Do Not Track (DNT) standard to inform websites of a user's preference not to be tracked, implemented in version 23; the protocol is turned off by default in Chrome, in line with the W3C draft standard. Chrome uses a multi-process architecture where each site instance and plugin runs in a separate process, known as process isolation, enhancing security and stability by preventing interference between tasks; an attacker gaining access to one tab cannot access others, and a crash in one instance results in a "Sad Tab" screen instead of a full browser crash; this architecture reduces memory fragmentation over time and was later adopted by Safari and Firefox. Chrome includes a Task Manager that allows users to monitor memory usage, download volume, and CPU consumption by sites and plugins and to terminate them; Chrome version 23 improved battery life on systems with GPU-accelerated video decoding. The first production release occurred on December 11, 2008, ending the initial beta period and beginning production; on January 8, 2009, Google introduced a three-channel release system: Stable, Beta, and Developer (Dev), replacing the previous two channels; all Developer users were moved to Beta, with Dev builds becoming less stable. Each channel has a distinct release cycle and stability level: Stable updates roughly quarterly with features and fixes that passed thorough Beta testing, Beta updates monthly with stable features migrated from Dev, and Dev updates once or twice weekly, exposing new features that may be unstable. In July 2010, Google shortened the Stable release cycle from quarterly to six weeks; Beta releases followed at a similar rate, one month earlier, and Dev releases occurred weekly or biweekly, allowing time for basic testing. A fourth channel, Canary, was introduced, updated daily from a build at 09:00 UTC from the most stable of the last 40 revisions, named after the canary-in-a-coal-mine practice to detect crashes; if a Canary build fails, it is blocked from migrating to Dev until fixed. Canary is the most bleeding-edge official version of Chrome, running side by side with other channels and allowing different profiles, themes, and preferences; it does not natively become the default browser, though it can be set via System Preferences on Windows and macOS. Canary was initially Windows-only, with a macOS version released on May 3, 2011. The Chrome beta channel for Android launched on January 10, 2013, running side by side with the stable channel; Chrome Dev for Android launched on April 29, 2015. Chrome channels are automatically distributed according to their release cycles; on Windows, updates are managed via Google Update, controllable via Group Policy; users can also download standalone installers that do not auto-update. On macOS, updates are managed via Google Update Service, controllable via macOS "defaults"; on Linux, updates are handled by the system's package manager. This auto-updating behavior contrasts with Chromium, the open-source core of Chrome, which provides continuous source code builds and requires users to manage their own updates. In March 2021, Google announced that starting with Chrome 94 in the third quarter of 2021, Stable releases would occur every four weeks instead of six weeks since 2010, and a new release channel for system administrators and browser embedders with eight-week releases was introduced. Releases are identified by a four-part version number, e.g., 42.0.2311.90 (Windows Stable release April 14, 2015); the components are major.minor.build.patch. Chromium and Chrome release schedules are linked through annual Branch Point dates, which precede the final Developer build release by four days and the Stable initial release by about 53 days. For example, the version 42 Branch Point was on February 20, 2015; Developer builds stopped at build 2311 with release 42.0.2311.4 on February 24 (four days later); the first Stable release, 42.0.2311.90, was on April 14, 2015 (53 days after the Branch Point). Chrome supports color management using system-provided ICC v2 and v4 support on macOS and ICC v2 profiles by default on other platforms starting from version 22. When not connected to the internet, Chrome displays an "8-bit" Tyrannosaurus rex on the "No internet" error screen; pressing the space bar, clicking, or tapping the T-Rex causes it to jump and dash across a cactus-ridden desert, revealing it as an Easter egg in the form of an infinite runner game with no time limit and periodic black tinting; school or enterprise managers can disable the game. As of April 2016, stable 32-bit and 64-bit builds are available for Windows, with only 64-bit stable builds available for Linux and macOS; 64-bit Windows builds became available in the developer channel and as Canary builds on June 3, 2014, in the beta channel on July 30.

When Chrome is not connected to the Internet and displays a "No internet" message, an "8-bit" Tyrannosaurus rex appears at the top of the screen; pressing the space bar, clicking it with a mouse, or tapping it on touch devices causes the T-Rex to jump and dash across a cactus-filled desert, revealing it as an Easter egg in the form of a platform game. The game is an infinite runner with no time limit, progressing faster over time and periodically tinting to a black background. A school or enterprise manager can disable this game. As of April 2016, stable 32-bit and 64-bit builds of Chrome are available for Windows, with only 64-bit stable builds available for Linux and macOS. 64-bit Windows builds became available in the developer channel on June 3, 2014, in the beta channel on July 30, 2014, and in the stable channel on August 26, 2014. 64-bit macOS builds became available as canary builds on November 7, 2013, in the beta channel on October 9, 2014, and in the stable channel on November 18, 2014. Starting with version 89, Chrome will only be supported on Intel/Intel x86 and AMD processors with the SSE3 instruction set. A beta version for Android 4.0 devices was launched on February 7, 2012, available in a limited number of countries via Google Play. Notable features include synchronization with desktop Chrome for shared bookmarks and tabs, page pre-rendering, and hardware acceleration. Chrome supports many HTML5 features such as GPU-accelerated canvas, CSS 3D Transforms, CSS animations, SVG, WebSocket (including binary messages), Dedicated Workers, overflow scroll, strong HTML5 video support, IndexedDB, WebWorkers, Application Cache, File APIs, date- and time-pickers, and parts of the Media Capture API. Mobile customizations include swipe gesture tab switching, link preview with zooming to ensure the correct link is clicked, and font size boosting for readability. Features missing in the mobile version include sandboxed tabs, Safe Browsing, apps or extensions, Adobe Flash (now and in the future), Native Client, and the ability to export user data like open tabs or browsing history into portable files. Development changes include remote debugging and part of the browser layer being implemented in Java, communicating with Chromium and WebKit via Java Native Bindings; Chrome for Android is a fork of the Chromium project, with a priority to upstream new and modified code to Chromium and WebKit. The April 17, 2012, update added support for 31 additional languages and availability in all countries where Google Play is available, allowing users to request a desktop version of a website instead of a mobile one, and enabling Android users to add bookmarks to their home screens and choose which apps handle links. On June 27, 2012, Chrome for Android exited beta and became stable. Chrome 18.0.1026311, released on September 26, 2012, was the first version to support mobile devices based on Intel x86. Starting from version 25, the Chrome version for Android aligns with the desktop version, with new stable releases available simultaneously. A separate Chrome for Android beta channel was launched on January 10, 2013, with version 25, and as of 2013, a separate beta version is available in the Google Play Store and can run alongside the stable release. Chrome is available on Apple's iOS and iPadOS, released on June 26, 2012, supporting iPad, iPhone, and formerly iPod touch; the current version requires iOS 17.0 or greater or iPadOS 17.0 or greater. Due to Apple's App Store requirements, this version uses iOS WebKit, Apple's rendering engine, and thus cannot use Google's V8 JavaScript engine. Chrome is the default browser for the iOS and iPadOS Gmail app. In a Chitika review from July 18, 2012, Chrome had 1.5% of the iOS browser market; by October 2013, it had 3% of the market. On Linux, 32-bit Intel processor support ended in March 2016, though Chromium remains supported; as of Chrome version 26, Linux installations require GCC v4.6 and GTK v2.24 or later, making systems like Debian 6 (2.20) and RHEL 6 (2.18) deprecated. Support for Chrome on Windows XP and Vista ended in April 2016; the last version compatible with these systems was Chrome 49.0.2623.112, released on April 7, 2016, and re-released on April 11, 2016. Support for Windows 7 was initially set to end on July 15, 2021, but was moved back to January 15, 2022, then again to January 15, 2023, due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and enterprise migration delays; support for Windows 7, 8, and 8.1 ended on this date, with Chrome 109 being the last version supporting these operating systems. "Windows 8 mode" was introduced in 2012 for the developer channel, enabling a full-screen, tablet-optimized interface with snapping, sharing, and search features; it was changed in October 2013 to use a desktop-like ChromeOS interface with a dedicated windowing system and taskbar, and was removed in version 49, with users upgrading to Windows 10 losing this feature. Google dropped support for Mac OS X 10.5 with Chrome 22; 32-bit Chrome support ended in November 2014 with Chrome 39; support for Mac OS X 10.6, 10.7, and 10.8 ended in April 2016 with Chrome 50; support for OS X 10.9 ended in April 2018 with Chrome 66; OS X 10.10 ended in January 2021 with Chrome 88; OS X 10.11 and macOS 10.12 ended in August 2022 with Chrome 104; macOS 10.13 and 10.14 ended in September 2023 with Chrome 117; macOS 10.15 ended in September 2024 with Chrome 129; macOS 11 ended in August 2025 with Chrome 139. Google Chrome is the foundation of ChromeOS, which ships on hardware from Google's manufacturing partners, featuring a minimalist interface resembling the Chrome browser and being designed for users who spend most of their time online; the only applications are a browser with media player and file manager. Google announced ChromeOS on July 7, 2009. Upon release, Chrome received acclaim; Matthew Moore of The Daily Telegraph noted it was "attractive, fast and has some impressive new features." Initially, Microsoft downplayed the threat from Chrome, predicting most users would stick with Internet Explorer 8, while Opera said Chrome would strengthen the web. By February 25, 2010, BusinessWeek reported that Google's Chrome had forced Microsoft to re-engage with browser development after years of inactivity. Mozilla stated Chrome's entry was not surprising and that it would not affect Google's revenue relationship with Mozilla. Chrome's design bridges desktop and cloud computing by allowing desktop, Start menu, or QuickLaunch shortcuts to any web page or application, blurring the line between online and desktop experiences. Google has been accused of using Chrome and Blink to promote in-house web standards implemented first in its services, leading to performance issues and compatibility problems, with some developers refusing to test on other browsers. Tom Warren of The Verge compared Chrome to Internet Explorer 6 due to its ubiquity. In 2021, computer scientist and lawyer Jonathan Mayer stated Chrome has become an agent for Google LLC rather than a user agent, lacking meaningful privacy protections, pushing users toward Google Account linking, and implementing invasive advertising. A class-action lawsuit seeking $5 billion in damages was filed in 2020 over misleading claims about incognito mode tracking; in December 2023, a settlement was agreed upon and filed in federal court on April 1, 2024, requiring Google to delete billions of browsing records, revise disclosures about data collection in incognito mode, and allow users to block third-party cookies for five years, without monetary damages and pending court approval. In June 2015, the Debian developer community discovered that Chromium 43 and Chrome 43 were programmed to download the Hotword Shared Module, which could enable the OK Google voice recognition extension, though it was off by default, raising privacy concerns; the module was removed in Chrome 45, released on September 1, 2015, and was only present in Chrome 43 and 44. Chrome sends user activity details to Google through both optional and non-optional tracking mechanisms. Some tracking features can be enabled or disabled during installation or through browser settings; unofficial builds like SRWare Iron aim to remove these features. The RLZ library, used to measure marketing success, is not included in the Chromium browser. In March 2010, Chrome began using a unique ID token for installation statistics only on the first connection made by Google Update. The optional suggestion service, which sends typed text in the Omnibox to search providers before return, has been criticized for providing search engines with IP-addressed web use data. Chrome previously suggested similar pages when a page was not found, contacting Google servers for this, a feature that has since been removed. A 2019 Washington Post review by Geoffrey A. Fowler found that Chrome stores thousands more cookies than Mozilla Firefox in a typical week, noting Google's financial interest in collecting user data and recommending a switch to Firefox, Safari, or Chromium-based Brave. On installation, tracking can be disabled in ChromeOS; for other operating systems, it can be disabled through the installation interface or browser options. In 2023, Google proposed a technology to "hide the IP and traffic of its users" by routing Chrome traffic to Google servers, drawing criticism as all traffic remains accessible to Google. Chrome is tied to Google's advertising business, which introduced FLoC and later Topics to replace third-party cookies and Manifest V3 API changes for extensions. In January 2021, Google announced progress on privacy-friendly alternatives to replace third-party cookies, promising to phase them out by 2022 with FLoC; this triggered antitrust investigations by the U.K.'s Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission, and drew criticism from DuckDuckGo, Brave, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation for underestimating user tracking capabilities. On January 25, 2022, Google announced the end of FLoC development and the introduction of the Topics API as a replacement, which uses weekly web activity to determine five interests, refreshing every three weeks and not retaining data. Manifest V3 has faced criticism for changes to the WebRequest API used by ad blockers and privacy extensions, with the declarative version processing rules in the browser instead of sending all traffic through extensions, improving performance but limiting rule count and expression types. The prohibition of remotely-hosted code restricts filter list updates, and due to the Chrome Web Store's fixed review process, updates may not be timely. Google has been accused of using Manifest V3 to hinder ad-blocking software due to its interest in the advertising market. In June 2019, Google increased the rule cap from 30,000 to 150,000 entries to address concerns about filtering limitations.

The WebRequest API enables ad blocking and privacy extensions to block and modify network connections, with its declarative version, DeclarativeWebRequest, processing rules directly within the browser instead of routing all traffic through the extension—a change Google claimed would improve performance. However, DeclarativeWebRequest is limited in the number of rules that can be set and the types of expressions allowed, and the prohibition of remotely-hosted code restricts independent updates to filter lists, which may not be updated promptly due to the fixed length of Chrome Web Store reviews. Google has faced criticism for using Manifest V3 to hinder ad-blocking software, citing performance issues and malicious extension use; in June 2019, it increased the rule cap from 30,000 to 150,000 entries to address concerns. In 2021, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) stated Manifest V3 was "outright harmful to privacy efforts" due to its impact on ad-blocking functionality. In December 2022, Google paused the transition to Manifest V3 to address developer feedback and migration issues, resuming it in November 2023, with support for Manifest V2 extensions removed from non-stable Chrome builds starting June 2024 and full removal from the Chrome Web Store in June 2025. These changes affected other Chromium-based browsers like Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi; Microsoft chose to support MV2 adblockers, while Brave maintained MV2 support as long as possible, though its reliance on the Chrome Web Store limited this, eventually creating a separate section for downloading MV2 extensions such as AdGuard, uBlock Origin, uMatrix, and NoScript. Mozilla stated it is adding Manifest V3 support to Firefox’s Chrome extension API for compatibility but emphasized that its implementation would not impose limitations on privacy or content-blocking extensions and that MV2 support would not be deprecated. Some developers released MV3 versions of their extensions, such as uBlock Origin Lite (uBOL), which features a static filter list, slower threat response, exclusion of filters for smaller or regional sites, absence of default cosmetic filters, and fewer overall filters; similar restrictions were introduced in Ghostry, Adblock Plus MV3, AdGuard MV3, and Stands MV3. Researchers from Goethe University Frankfurt found that MV3 extension providers largely bypassed Google’s restrictions, with tested MV3 versions blocking as many or more requests to trackers and ads than their MV2 counterparts, though cosmetic filters were over 20% less effective. In August 2024, a U.S. federal judge ruled Google maintained an illegal monopoly over search services, and in November 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice demanded Google sell Chrome to end its search monopoly. On August 12, 2025, Perplexity AI made a $34.5 billion bid to acquire Chrome from Google, claiming the sale could resolve ongoing antitrust litigation. Chrome overtook Firefox in November 2011 in global usage, and as of January 2026, according to StatCounter, it held a 71% global usage share (Cloudflare reported 68%), making it the most widely used web browser. On Sunday, March 18, 2012, Chrome first became the most used browser globally, securing 32.7% of web browsing, just ahead of Internet Explorer at 32.5%. From May 14 to 21, 2012, Chrome generated more internet traffic than Internet Explorer for the first time, with 31.88% and 31.47% of traffic respectively, marking the first week-long lead. At the 2012 Google I/O conference, Google reported 310 million active Chrome users, nearly double the 160 million in 2011. In June 2013, Chrome overtook Internet Explorer for the first time in the U.S. In August 2013, 43% of global internet users used Chrome, with Statista noting 36% in North America—the lowest globally. In December 2010, Google introduced an official Chrome MSI package for business use, which allows system-level installation and administrator control over updates, unlike the standard user-level installer that places Chrome in the local app data directory and enables invisible background updates; the MSI package, initially limited, was enhanced with group policy objects to fine-tune Chrome behavior, with over 500 policies now available. Google launched Chrome Browser Enterprise Support in 2016, a paid service for IT administrators to access expert support, and Chrome Browser Cloud Management in 2019, a dashboard enabling IT managers to control content, app usage, and installed extensions. In September 2008, Google released a significant portion of Chrome’s source code as the open-source project Chromium, enabling third-party developers to study and port the browser to macOS and Linux; the Google-authored portion is under the permissive BSD license, while other parts are under various open-source licenses. Chromium is similar to Chrome but lacks built-in automatic updates, a built-in Flash player, Google branding, and has a blue logo instead of the multicolored Google logo; it does not implement user RLZ tracking. Initially, the Chrome PDF viewer, PDFium, was excluded from Chromium but was made open-source in May 2014 and can be used to fill PDF forms. Applications, extensions, and themes for Chrome are developed and packaged in .crx files containing a manifest.json file specifying version, name, description, privileges, and other UI elements like icons and popups, with Google providing an official developer guide for creation and publishing. Chrome has its own web store for uploading and downloading these tools. As with Internet Explorer, Chrome’s popularity has led to malware abuse, such as the adware "eFast" that appeared in late 2015, which mimicked Chrome’s appearance, hijacked file associations, and injected ads into web pages.
